weekLabel: Week 2 · Meeting A · Values and Expressions

slides.title: Give architectural quantities meaning in Python
slides.subtitle: Types, names, operators, units, strings, comparisons, and transparent calculations
slides.teaching: Display 12, 12.0, and '12'. Ask whether they mean the same thing to Python and whether an unlabeled 12 means anything in a drawing set.

slides.title: A number without meaning is weak design data
slides.statement: A useful variable connects a value to a concept, a unit, and an intended operation.
slides.supporting: Naming and type choices are modeling decisions: they determine what the program can safely do next.
slides.teaching: Connect variable names to architectural annotation. A dimension is not useful if its unit or referent is ambiguous.

outcomes.head: Classify
outcomes.body: Recognize integer, float, string, Boolean, and None values.

outcomes.head: Name
outcomes.body: Create readable variables carrying architectural meaning and units.

outcomes.head: Calculate
outcomes.body: Use operators, precedence, conversion, comparison, and formatting.

outcomes.head: Validate
outcomes.body: Test a calculation with known, boundary, and invalid cases.

slides.teaching: Tie each outcome to the facade opening-ratio model developed near the end.

items: Tests expose unit and logic mistakes
slides.teaching: Explain that syntax will be introduced only when it supports the cumulative architectural calculation.

slides.title: Quantities become credible as meaning and checks accumulate

tiers.task: Calculate a 12.0 m × 3.0 m wall area and identify the result's type.
Convert 25.0 ft to meters with the named factor ft_to_m = 0.3048.
Find 42/(18×9), then test 200/(18×9). Explain why the second result needs a geometry rule.

slides.teaching: Ask students to name what is added at each level: type, conversion provenance, then a validity rule. A numerical result can be correctly computed and still represent impossible geometry.

slides.title: A data type is a category of value and behavior

left.head: Common beginning types
left.body:
int — whole numbers
float — decimal numbers
str — text
bool — True or False
None — no value yet

right.head: Architectural examples
right.body:
floor_count = 4
height_m = 3.6
material = 'brick'
is_exterior = True
result = None

slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L4 slides 2–12. Type is behavior, not formatting. Ask which values can be multiplied, labeled, or tested as a condition. The next two slides take int and float one at a time.

slides.title: Integers count things that cannot be split
slides.definition: A whole number with no decimal point: 0, 3, -2, 48. Use int for anything you count rather than measure — storeys, rooms, panels, occupants, parking spaces. Choosing int is a modeling claim: it says half of one of these would be meaningless. Arithmetic between two ints stays int, so 12 * 3 is 36, never 36.0.

example.head: floor_count = 4
example.body:
Four storeys — not 4.0 storeys. A building cannot have four and a half of them, so the whole number is the honest representation. Compare that with a measured storey height, where the decimals carry real information.

Test a quantity by asking whether half of one would mean anything. Half an occupant does not; half a metre does.

slides.note: 4 and 4.0 are not the same object. They compare as equal, but their types differ, and type is what decides which operations are available.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L4 slides 7–8. Ask for three architectural quantities that must be int and three that must not. Hold binary approximation for the later precision slide.

slides.title: Floating-point values measure quantities that vary
slides.definition: A number stored with a decimal point: 3.6, 0.125, -0.5. Use float for measured or calculated quantities — lengths, areas, ratios, costs. Division with / always produces a float, even when the answer looks whole: 8 / 2 is 4.0, not 4. Mixing the types also produces a float, so 12 + 3.6 is 15.6.

example.head: height_m = 3.6
example.body:
A storey height is measured, so its decimals carry information. Every quantity calculated from it — wall area, opening ratio, cost per square metre — is also a float, because one measured value turns the whole chain into float arithmetic.

Writing 3.6 rather than 4 is a claim about the survey, not about tidiness.

slides.note: Floating point describes how the value is stored in binary, not how many decimals you see. Python fixes the type; the digits printed are a separate choice made later.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L4 slides 7–8. Demonstrate 8 / 2 in the Console and ask why Python answers 4.0. Note that / is the one operator that always widens int to float.

slides.title: Use type() to inspect what Python sees
slides.code:
floor_count = 4
height_m = 3.6
material = 'brick'
is_exterior = True
result = None

print(type(floor_count), type(height_m))
print(type(material), type(is_exterior), type(result))
slides.explainBody: Do not guess during debugging. type(value) reports the object type and is especially useful after input, file loading, or AI-generated code. None's type prints as NoneType — the two spellings name the value and its type.
slides.teaching: Run each print separately first, one type() at a time, then show the grouped version. Connect every reported type to the operations that type allows.

slides.title: A literal is a value written directly in the script
slides.definition: A value typed straight into your code instead of being calculated, converted, or read from a file. 4 is an integer literal, 3.6 a float literal, 'brick' a string literal, True a Boolean literal, and None is the literal that stands for no value yet.

example.head: height_m = 3.6
example.body:
3.6 is the literal; height_m is the name. A literal supplies raw data and a name supplies context. The literal 3.6 becomes architectural evidence only when a name, a unit, an assumption, and a source explain what it represents.

Every number in today's facade calculation begins as a literal that somebody typed.

slides.note: Quotes decide the type: 3.6 is a float literal, '3.6' is a string literal. They look almost identical in the Editor and behave completely differently.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3 slides 9–13 and 21. Ask students to identify every literal in the opening-ratio example built later today.

slides.title: Recall: reassigning a name does not rewrite the past
slides.definition: Recall from Week 1A: a variable is a name bound to a value by assignment, not mathematical equality — Python evaluates the right side first, then binds the name on the left to that result. Writing the same name again does not edit the old value in place: it makes the name refer to a new value, and anything already computed from the earlier value keeps its old result until you recompute it.

example.head: length_m = 9.0
example.body:
Reassignment. Writing this later makes the same name refer to a different value; the earlier 8.5 is simply no longer reachable through that name. Nothing you already calculated from length_m changes on its own.

Watch the Variable Explorer as this line runs: one row, one new value.

slides.note: A variable is not a live formula. If area_m2 was calculated from length_m, changing length_m afterwards leaves area_m2 at its old value until you rerun that line.
slides.teaching: Students met variable/assignment in Week 1A (see week01a.json slide 22); do not re-derive the base definition here — name it and move straight to the reassignment/stale-value angle, which is new. The next slide takes one assignment apart part by part.

slides.title: Read an assignment from the right side back to the name

parts.label: The new name
parts.body: Created by this line. Nothing was stored here before.

parts.label: Assignment
parts.body: Read it as 'becomes'. It never asks whether two things match.

parts.label: Looked up
parts.body: Python replaces the name with the value it holds now.

parts.label: The operator
parts.body: m times m gives m², so the unit changes here too.

parts.label: Unchanged
parts.body: Reading a name never alters it. Only the left side is set.

slides.teaching: Walk the numbered parts in order 3, 4, 5, 2, 1 — right side first, then the assignment, then the name. Ask for the unit of the result before anyone gives a number.

slides.title: Assignment evaluates the right side first
slides.code:
length_m = 8.5
width_m = 5.2
area_m2 = length_m * width_m

width_m = 6.0
print(area_m2)
slides.explainBody: area_m2 keeps the earlier result. Changing width_m later does not recalculate prior statements. Execution order creates program state.
slides.teaching: Ask whether the output is 44.2 or 51.0 and require an explanation rather than a vote.

slides.title: Names should reveal concept and unit

left.head: Readable (snake_case)
left.body:
snake_case: lowercase words joined by underscores, e.g. wall_height_m.

wall_height_m
window_area_m2
floor_count
is_accessible

right.head: Risky
right.body:
Legal but poor style:
h
value1
windowAreaInSquareMetersMaybe

Illegal — SyntaxError:
2nd_floor
class

slides.teaching: Explain snake_case, no leading digit, and reserved words. Distinguish illegal syntax (2nd_floor, class) from merely poor style (h, value1). Communication is the goal; legal syntax alone is insufficient.

slides.title: Arithmetic operators encode the calculation
slides.code:
wall_area_m2 = 12 * 3.0
opening_area_m2 = 1.8 * 2.0
net_area_m2 = wall_area_m2 - opening_area_m2
ratio = opening_area_m2 / wall_area_m2
panels = 4 ** 2

print(net_area_m2, ratio, panels)
slides.explainBody: + adds, - subtracts, * multiplies, / divides, ** exponentiates. An expression combines values, variables, and operators to produce a new value.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 operator slides 3–4. Students narrate the meaning and unit of every result before the code is run.

slides.title: Multiplication happens before subtraction, always
slides.code:
gross_m2 = 12 * 3
opening_m2 = 6
openings = 2

net_m2 = gross_m2 - opening_m2 * openings
print(net_m2)
slides.question: What does this print?
slides.why: * runs before -, so two 6 m² openings come off the wall. Reading left to right gives 60. int stays int.
slides.teaching: Take a show of hands on every option before revealing. 60 is the left-to-right reading, 30 forgets the count of openings, 24.0 assumes every calculation returns a float. Then run it in the Console.

slides.title: Precedence determines which operation happens first
slides.explainBody: Exponentiation precedes multiplication and division; those precede addition and subtraction. Parentheses override the default order and communicate the intended grouping.
slides.teaching: Students translate each expression into a short verbal procedure, then connect it back to the wall-and-openings prediction.

slides.title: Units are part of the data model
slides.statement: Python can multiply 10 feet by 3 meters without objecting.
slides.supporting: A successful execution does not guarantee a meaningful architectural result. Encode units in names, normalize inputs, and label outputs.
slides.teaching: Establish the class convention: measured quantities carry units in variable names.

slides.title: Convert units explicitly and preserve provenance
slides.code:
length_ft = 25
feet_to_m = 0.3048
length_m = length_ft * feet_to_m

print(length_m)
slides.explainBody: Keep the original value, name the factor, store the converted result with its new unit, and compare with a rough estimate. Do not overwrite away the source value.
slides.teaching: Estimate first: 25 feet is a little over 7 meters. Ask where the conversion factor came from.

slides.title: Similar-looking values can have different types
rows: a whole number; arithmetic is available
one text character; quotes make it text
a truth value used by decisions
slides.callout: Type belongs to the value, not to the visual appearance of the characters.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L4. Ask students to predict 5 * 2 versus '5' * 2. The answers are 10 and '55': the second repeats the text twice.

slides.title: A string is text enclosed in quotes
slides.code:
room = 'Studio'
level = "Second Floor"
label = room + ' — ' + level

print(label)
slides.explainBody: A string stores letters, digits, symbols, and spaces as text. Single or double quotes delimit it. + concatenates strings; arithmetic requires a numerical type.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3 slide 13 and L4 slide 6. Connect strings to room names, IDs, material categories, filenames, and annotations.

slides.title: f-strings make calculated output readable
slides.code:
room = 'Studio'
area_m2 = 44.234

message = f'{room}: {area_m2:.1f} m²'
print(message)
slides.explainBody: Prefix the string with f. Place expressions inside braces. :.1f requests one decimal place. Formatting changes display—not the stored number or its accuracy.
slides.teaching: Have students point to the underlying value, display precision, and unit suffix. The next slide takes this exact line apart.

slides.title: An f-string is a template with slots for values

parts.label: The f prefix
parts.body: Without the f, the braces would print as literal braces.

parts.label: A slot
parts.body: The value of room is looked up and dropped in as text.

parts.label: Value + format
parts.body: The same slot, with :.1f added to show one decimal.

parts.label: Literal text
parts.body: Anything outside the braces prints exactly as written.

slides.teaching: Point at part 3 and stress that area_m2 still holds 44.234; :.1f changed the display only. Ask what :.2f, :.0f, and :.1% would each show.

slides.title: Text input must become a number before calculation
slides.explainBody: input() returns text. float(text) converts compatible decimal text; int(text) converts compatible whole-number text. Invalid text raises an error and must be handled deliberately.
slides.teaching: Use a live input example and distinguish conversion from validation.

slides.title: A Boolean stores one of two truth values
slides.code:
has_daylight = True
needs_review = False

print(has_daylight)
print(type(needs_review))
slides.explainBody: bool is Python's yes-or-no data type. True and False use capital first letters and no quotation marks. They often result from comparisons and control later decisions.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3 slide 21, L4 slides 11–12, and L7 slides 2–3. Ask for architectural yes/no questions.

slides.title: Comparison operators ask precise yes-or-no questions
slides.callout: Every comparison evaluates to the Boolean value True or False. = assigns; == compares.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L7 slide 5 and Lxx Operator slide 7. Translate each operator into spoken language before showing code.

slides.title: Comparisons produce Boolean evidence
slides.code:
area_m2 = 44.2
minimum_m2 = 40.0

meets_minimum = area_m2 >= minimum_m2
print(meets_minimum)
slides.explainHead: Comparison is not a decision yet
slides.explainBody: The expression area_m2 >= minimum_m2 asks one question and returns True or False. It records evidence; a conditional statement introduced next week decides what action follows.
slides.teaching: Contrast = and ==. Ask what assumptions are hidden in a single minimum-area threshold.

slides.title: Conversion can change meaning or lose information

right.head: Questions before conversion
right.body:
Is the source value valid?
Does truncation make sense?
Are units preserved?
Does the result need rounding only for display?

slides.teaching: Emphasize that int(4.8) truncates rather than rounding. Conversion is a modeling choice.

slides.title: Two values that look equal can fail an equality test
slides.code:
# two 100 mm increments of a 300 mm grid
module_m = 0.1 + 0.2
target_m = 0.3

print(module_m == target_m)
slides.question: What does this print?
slides.why: 0.1 + 0.2 is stored as 0.30000000000000004, so the exact test fails. Compare rounded values, not raw floats.
slides.teaching: Almost everyone predicts True. Do not explain first — run it, then show the stored value on the next slide. Option C confuses == with =; option D assumes floats cannot be compared at all.

slides.title: Floating-point display is not measurement accuracy
slides.explainBody: Computers approximate many decimal fractions in binary. round() or formatting controls displayed precision. Neither repairs inaccurate inputs or weak assumptions.
slides.teaching: Distinguish computational representation, display precision, and real measurement accuracy. round() returns a new value; it does not repair module_m.

slides.title: Worked example: one facade against a code limit
slides.code:
max_ratio = 0.40

north_width_m = 18.0
north_height_m = 9.0
north_window_m2 = 42.0
north_area_m2 = north_width_m * north_height_m
north_ratio = north_window_m2 / north_area_m2
north_ok = north_ratio <= max_ratio

print(f'North: {north_ratio:.1%}  meets code: {north_ok}')
slides.explainHead: Naming the limit turns a number into a rule
slides.explainBody: :.1% is new: like :.1f, but it also multiplies by 100 and appends a percent sign for display only. max_ratio is named once so every facade can be checked against the identical rule — no facade gets a private, undocumented threshold.
slides.teaching: Trace units: m × m produces m²; m² / m² produces a dimensionless ratio. Ask what happens if the window area were larger before revealing the next slide.

slides.title: ...continued: check a second, real condition
slides.code:
west_width_m = 12.0
west_height_m = 9.0
west_window_m2 = 54.0
west_area_m2 = west_width_m * west_height_m
west_ratio = west_window_m2 / west_area_m2
west_ok = west_ratio <= max_ratio

print(f'North: {north_ratio:.1%}  meets code: {north_ok}')
print(f'West:  {west_ratio:.1%}  meets code: {west_ok}')
slides.output:
North: 25.9%  meets code: True
West:  50.0%  meets code: False
slides.explainBody: Comparing each facade's ratio against the SAME named max_ratio — not a copy-pasted, re-typed threshold — is exactly the 'compare real design conditions' move Project 1 will ask for. The model still assumes one rectangular gross facade per elevation and ignores glazing type, shading, and thermal performance.
slides.teaching: Ask why West fails and North doesn't — same rule, different geometry, nothing arbitrary about which one is called out.

slides.title: Test cases should include answers you already know
slides.callout: Known-answer and boundary tests make hidden mistakes visible before a model grows. Write one as code: assert round(opening_ratio, 2) == 0.5 halts the script the moment the model disagrees.
slides.teaching: Students compute expected answers without Python and decide whether the excessive area should raise a warning or stop execution. Introduce assert here: it states a claim you expect to be true, does nothing when it passes, and stops the script when it fails. Round before comparing floats, per the previous two slides.

slides.title: Trace types as well as values
slides.callout: The same conceptual quantity can move through representations. Trace what each conversion enables and what it may hide.
slides.teaching: Have students identify where calculation becomes possible and where the result becomes presentation text.

slides.title: Audit an AI-generated quantity calculator
slides.prompt: AI returns: wall = '12'; height = 3; area = wall * height; print(area + ' m²')
steps: Predict what each operation attempts and what actually happens.
Identify the type error and the misleading intermediate value.
Rewrite with unit-aware names, explicit conversion, and an f-string.
Add one known-answer assertion and one invalid-input test.
slides.teaching: Expected repair: wall_m = float(wall) = 12.0; area_m2 = wall_m * height = 36.0; print(f'{area_m2} m²') → '36.0 m²'. The bug: wall is a string, so wall * height triggers string repetition ('12' * 3 = '121212'), and print(area + ' m²') still succeeds — no crash, just a silently wrong number concatenated with the unit text. That is why step 2 calls it a type error rather than a runtime error: the script runs to completion and looks fine at a glance. Verified in the Python console: '12' * 3 == '121212'; float('12') * 3 == 36.0. Require an assert for the known input (wall='12', height=3 → 36.0) and a test that a non-numeric wall value is rejected or raises clearly.

slides.title: Meaning travels with type, name, and unit
takeaways: Parentheses and conversion make intent explicit.
Known-answer and boundary tests expose plausible mistakes.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: rewrite one ambiguous quantity from today's work as a type-aware, unit-aware variable.
